claims.claim: Wolfe argues that Kay's whole career as a fantasy writer occupies the space between Graves's line that there is one story only worth telling and Berger's line that no single story will again be told as if it were the only one, and that Berger's position prevails.
claims.source: Gary K. Wolfe, "Guy Gavriel Kay: An Introduction", Journal of the Fantastic in the Arts 20.2 (2009)
claims.quote: in the end, I think John Berger wins

claims.claim: Wolfe characterises Kay as fascinated with the multiplicity of story since the start of his career.
claims.source: Gary K. Wolfe, "Guy Gavriel Kay: An Introduction", Journal of the Fantastic in the Arts 20.2 (2009)
claims.quote: fascinated with the multiplicity of story

claims.claim: Wolfe treats the epigraph and the closing quotation of Ysabel as the two poles framing the novel, quoting Berger's line from the end of the book.
claims.source: Gary K. Wolfe, "Guy Gavriel Kay: An Introduction", Journal of the Fantastic in the Arts 20.2 (2009)
claims.quote: Never again will a single story be told

claims.claim: Kay names his own opening baseball quotations as a deliberate unreliable-narrator device rather than digression.
claims.source: Guy Gavriel Kay, "The Fiction of Privacy: Fantasy and the Past", Journal of the Fantastic in the Arts 20.2 (2009)
claims.quote: a classic unreliable narrator device

claims.claim: Kay states the distinction Walter Scott offered for the use of real people in historical fiction: that they be background figures to the invented protagonists rather than viewpoint characters.
claims.source: Guy Gavriel Kay, "Reflections on an Ethical Society", address of 4 November 2000 (BrightWeavings, Kay's authorized site)
claims.quote: background figures to the invented protagonists, not viewpoint characters

claims.claim: Borowska-Szerszun argues the fantastic element in Kay's Al-Rassan and Sarantine novels is left vague and merely signalled rather than fully set out.
claims.source: Sylwia Borowska-Szerszun, "When Gods are Absent from Fantasy", in The Light of Life: Essays in Honour of Professor Barbara Kowalik (Libron, 2017)
claims.quote: signalled rather than fully outlined

claims.claim: Borowska-Szerszun observes that Kay spends much effort outlining the social and cultural context of these novels while leaving the fantastic vague.
claims.source: Sylwia Borowska-Szerszun, "When Gods are Absent from Fantasy", in The Light of Life: Essays in Honour of Professor Barbara Kowalik (Libron, 2017)
claims.quote: much effort is taken to outline the social and cultural context

claims.claim: Borowska-Szerszun states that in The Sarantine Mosaic ordinary people are barely aware, if at all, that history-changing events are taking place.
claims.source: Sylwia Borowska-Szerszun, "When Gods are Absent from Fantasy", in The Light of Life: Essays in Honour of Professor Barbara Kowalik (Libron, 2017)
claims.quote: with ordinary people being barely, if at all, aware

claims.claim: Borowska-Szerszun describes the Sarantine duology's focalizers as ranging from aristocrats and senators through merchants and craftsmen to charioteers, soldiers, servants and foreigners.
claims.source: Sylwia Borowska-Szerszun, "When Gods are Absent from Fantasy", in The Light of Life: Essays in Honour of Professor Barbara Kowalik (Libron, 2017)
claims.quote: aristocrats and senators, through merchants and craftsmen, to charioteers

claims.claim: Borowska-Szerszun argues Kay depicts religions as social and political constructs made by people rather than by gods.
claims.source: Sylwia Borowska-Szerszun, "When Gods are Absent from Fantasy", in The Light of Life: Essays in Honour of Professor Barbara Kowalik (Libron, 2017)
claims.quote: social and political constructs created by humans rather than gods

claims.claim: Borowska-Szerszun states that in Kay's narratives the fantastic habitually gives way to the mimetic mode of representation.
claims.source: Sylwia Borowska-Szerszun, "When Gods are Absent from Fantasy", in The Light of Life: Essays in Honour of Professor Barbara Kowalik (Libron, 2017)
claims.quote: the fantastic habitually gives way to the mimetic mode

claims.claim: Kay says he realised early in shaping Children of Earth and Sky that he wanted it to be a novel about not-powerful people.
claims.source: Guy Gavriel Kay interviewed by Sandra Alvarez, Medievalists.net (2016)
claims.quote: a novel about not-powerful people

claims.claim: Kay says he wanted to suggest that the lives of those not central to their time are as worth a writer's and a reader's attention as the shakers and movers.
claims.source: Guy Gavriel Kay interviewed by Sandra Alvarez, Medievalists.net (2016)
claims.quote: the lives of those not central to their time

claims.claim: Kay says his gateway into Tang China was its poets rather than its political history.
claims.source: Guy Gavriel Kay interviewed by Sandra Alvarez, Medievalists.net (2016)
claims.quote: the astonishingly great poets of that time

claims.claim: Labrousse-Marchau argues that in A Song for Arbonne the gods function as focal points for religious faith and instruments of political manipulation rather than as present powers.
claims.source: Nathalie Labrousse-Marchau, "A Song for Arbonne: De-romanticised fantasy", trans. Francois Vincent (BrightWeavings)
claims.quote: focal points for religious faith, abstract and transcendent entities

claims.claim: Taylor identifies double-edged gifts, which deliver great benefits at an equally great cost, as one of the structuring oppositions of The Fionavar Tapestry.
claims.source: Dena Taylor, "The Double-Edged Gift: Power and Moral Choice in The Fionavar Tapestry" (BrightWeavings)
claims.quote: deliver great benefits at an equally great cost

claims.claim: Laszkiewicz argues that in high/epic fantasy, the four series she analyses including Kay's Fionavar Tapestry, the city is not of particular interest to the writers.
claims.source: Weronika Laszkiewicz, "Abandoning the Quest? High/Epic Fantasy and the Challenges of the Anthropocene", Atlantis 46.1 (2024)
claims.quote: the city is not of particular interest to its writers

claims.claim: Laszkiewicz argues that the cities of high/epic fantasy, Kay's Brennin among the examples she names, are presented as places of shelter and provisioning on the protagonist's journey.
claims.source: Weronika Laszkiewicz, "Abandoning the Quest? High/Epic Fantasy and the Challenges of the Anthropocene", Atlantis 46.1 (2024)
claims.quote: places of shelter and provisioning on the protagonist's journey

claims.claim: Laszkiewicz observes that these fantasy cities are seldom shown suffering the ailments common to modern cities, listing waste, housing, gentrification, green space and traffic.
claims.source: Weronika Laszkiewicz, "Abandoning the Quest? High/Epic Fantasy and the Challenges of the Anthropocene", Atlantis 46.1 (2024)
claims.quote: seldom shown suffering from the ailments common to modern cities

claims.claim: Laszkiewicz observes that where urban hardships do appear in these works they read as elements of the hero's experience of the city rather than as evidence of failed urban management.
claims.source: Weronika Laszkiewicz, "Abandoning the Quest? High/Epic Fantasy and the Challenges of the Anthropocene", Atlantis 46.1 (2024)
claims.quote: inherent elements of the hero's experience of the city

claims.claim: Laszkiewicz states that high/epic fantasy attends to the landscape in general, and to landmarks significant for the hero's quest, rather than to the city.
claims.source: Weronika Laszkiewicz, "Abandoning the Quest? High/Epic Fantasy and the Challenges of the Anthropocene", Atlantis 46.1 (2024)
claims.quote: pays attention to the landscape in general

claims.claim: Laszkiewicz credits high/epic fantasy's length and its world-building across centuries with the ability to present large-scale processes that no individual person notices.
claims.source: Weronika Laszkiewicz, "Abandoning the Quest? High/Epic Fantasy and the Challenges of the Anthropocene", Atlantis 46.1 (2024)
claims.quote: processes which go unnoticed by any individual person

claims.claim: Borowska-Szerszun reads Kay's account of the Heladikos controversy as pinpointing the arbitrariness of what a religious authority admits as official doctrine.
claims.source: Sylwia Borowska-Szerszun, "When Gods are Absent from Fantasy", in The Light of Life: Essays in Honour of Professor Barbara Kowalik (Libron, 2017)
claims.quote: pinpointing the arbitrariness of deciding on what is accepted

claims.claim: Borowska-Szerszun reports Malosse's observation that the Sarantine Mosaic's debt to sixth-century Byzantium is not disguised, real places appearing under transparent new names.
claims.source: Sylwia Borowska-Szerszun, "When Gods are Absent from Fantasy", in The Light of Life: Essays in Honour of Professor Barbara Kowalik (Libron, 2017)
claims.quote: the debt to the real sixth-century Byzantium is not at all disguised

claims.claim: Doherty judges Kay more frugal than Lawhead in his use of religious symbolism.
claims.source: John J. Doherty, "The High Fantasies of Lawhead and Kay" (BrightWeavings)
claims.quote: Kay is better, and more frugal, in his use of it

claims.claim: Clements argues that in Kay human choice can sometimes effect change against the Weaver's will rather than as its instrument, unlike free will in Tolkien.
claims.source: Susannah Clements, "From Middle Earth to Fionavar" (Conference on Christianity and Literature, 2002; BrightWeavings)
claims.quote: human choice is of such value that it can sometimes affect change

claims.claim: Cheryl Morgan writes that Kay built the Sarantine Mosaic prologue as a patchwork of people and places meant to set the scene.
claims.source: Cheryl Morgan, 'Pieces of History', Emerald City (reprinted BrightWeavings, posted 2016-05-07)
claims.quote: a patchwork of people and places designed to set the scene

claims.claim: Morgan calls Crispin a literary device: a lowly but conveniently placed observer through whom Kay tells a much greater tale.
claims.source: Cheryl Morgan, 'Pieces of History', Emerald City (reprinted BrightWeavings, posted 2016-05-07)
claims.quote: a lowly but conveniently placed observer

claims.claim: Christopher Cobb says Devin knows nothing of his land's true history, so the reader can learn that history as he learns it.
claims.source: Christopher Cobb, in Cobb and Mohanraj, 'From Tapestry to Mosaic', Strange Horizons, 13 November 2000
claims.quote: the reader can learn that history as he learns it

claims.claim: Cobb objects that on rereading Tigana the set-up of Catriana's death and recovery felt like narratorial sleight-of-hand.
claims.source: Christopher Cobb, in Cobb and Mohanraj, 'From Tapestry to Mosaic', Strange Horizons, 13 November 2000
claims.quote: I was being set up by narratorial sleight-of-hand

claims.claim: Cobb says Kay's plotting lets him treat the relations between ordinary people like Crispin and rulers like Valerius in a plausible way.
claims.source: Christopher Cobb, in Cobb and Mohanraj, 'We must learn to bend, or we break', Strange Horizons, 13 November 2000
claims.quote: ordinary people like Crispin, and rulers like Valerius

claims.claim: Kay says a researched detail is cut when it feels gratuitous or forced, or reads like the raw information dumps he dislikes in other people's books.
claims.source: Guy Gavriel Kay, interviewed by Sandy Auden, infinity plus, 3 July 2005
claims.quote: one of those raw information dumps I dislike in other

claims.claim: Simeon Shoul says Kay's prose has always been quite mannered and quite deliberately styled.
claims.source: Simeon Shoul, review of The Lions of Al-Rassan, infinity plus
claims.quote: a prose that has always been quite mannered, quite deliberately styled

claims.claim: Shoul complains that Kay as narrator will directly inform the reader that his characters are brilliant.
claims.source: Simeon Shoul, review of The Lions of Al-Rassan, infinity plus
claims.quote: as narrator, will directly inform us that they are brilliant

claims.claim: Shoul reports that Kay compresses a Reconquista that actually took about four hundred years into no more than thirty-five.
claims.source: Simeon Shoul, review of The Lions of Al-Rassan, infinity plus
claims.quote: Kay compresses it into no more than thirty-five

claims.claim: Shoul notes Kay uses a brief prologue and epilogue to sketch the beginnings and ends of the historical process the novel compresses.
claims.source: Simeon Shoul, review of The Lions of Al-Rassan, infinity plus
claims.quote: sketch the beginnings and ends of the process

claims.claim: Shoul says Crispin sees much, though not all, of the plots and affairs that drive the novel.
claims.source: Simeon Shoul, review of Lord of Emperors, infinity plus
claims.quote: Crispin sees much, though not all, of the varied

claims.claim: Auden says names like Halldr, Ceinion and Aeldred conjure their own ancient images.
claims.source: Sandy Auden, review of The Last Light of the Sun, infinity plus
claims.quote: conjure their own ancient images

claims.claim: Auden says Kay blends the present tense with unusual cadences to demonstrate the strangeness of the faeries.
claims.source: Sandy Auden, review of The Last Light of the Sun, infinity plus
claims.quote: blends the present tense with unusual cadences

claims.claim: Auden says Kay's use of speech drives the plot and illustrates his ninth-century world at the same time.
claims.source: Sandy Auden, review of The Last Light of the Sun, infinity plus
claims.quote: it drives the plot and illustrates his 9th Century

claims.claim: Auden describes the book as a prose spiral that starts with a wide vista of kingdoms and narrows until individual characters stand alone.
claims.source: Sandy Auden, review of The Last Light of the Sun, infinity plus
claims.quote: Starting with a wide vista concerning kingdoms

claims.claim: Kirkus says Kay spun a richly sensuous fantasy world full of evocative history, religions, folklore, local customs and magical rites.
claims.source: Kirkus Reviews, unsigned review of Tigana, issue of 15 August 1990
claims.quote: full of evocative history, religions, folklore, local customs, and magical rites

claims.claim: Kirkus says the novel's colorful setting nearly steals the show from its plot threads.
claims.source: Kirkus Reviews, unsigned review of Tigana, issue of 15 August 1990
claims.quote: the novel's colorful setting nearly steals the show

claims.claim: Kirkus says the reader sees Arbonne much of the time through the eyes of Blaise, an expatriate mercenary captain.
claims.source: Kirkus Reviews, unsigned review of A Song for Arbonne
claims.quote: we see Arbonne through the eyes of Blaise

claims.claim: Kirkus says the final pages leave the reader with the impression that the novel's events have abruptly receded into some long-forgotten history.
claims.source: Kirkus Reviews, unsigned review of The Lions of Al-Rassan
claims.quote: abruptly receded into some long-forgotten history

claims.claim: Kirkus says the complex characterization and richly detailed settings create an unusually full portrait of an exotic society.
claims.source: Kirkus Reviews, unsigned review of The Lions of Al-Rassan
claims.quote: richly detailed settings create an unusually full portrait

claims.claim: Kirkus says Kay narrates the empire's outcome drawing straight from the annals.
claims.source: Kirkus Reviews, unsigned review of River of Stars
claims.quote: drawing straight from the annals

claims.claim: Kirkus's verdict on River of Stars is that the book is lucid and lyrical, and skillfully written.
claims.source: Kirkus Reviews, unsigned review of River of Stars
claims.quote: Lucid and lyrical, and skillfully written

claims.claim: Kirkus complains that Kay draws back from the crux of climactic moments to muse on how small individual lives are.
claims.source: Kirkus Reviews, unsigned review of Children of Earth and Sky
claims.quote: drawing back from the crux of climactic moments

claims.claim: Kirkus calls the historical setting of Children of Earth and Sky lush, well-researched and well-painted.
claims.source: Kirkus Reviews, unsigned review of Children of Earth and Sky
claims.quote: The historical setting is lush, well-researched, and well-painted

claims.claim: Kirkus warns that Kay risks readers finding the history to be his strongest character.
claims.source: Kirkus Reviews, unsigned review of Children of Earth and Sky
claims.quote: readers finding the history to be his strongest character

claims.claim: Kirkus says Danio's silence enables the assassination's success and sets in motion the events that carry him to the courts of the powerful.
claims.source: Kirkus Reviews, unsigned review of A Brightness Long Ago, issue of 15 March 2019
claims.quote: Danio's silence enables the assassination's success

claims.claim: Publishers Weekly says the culture of River of Stars is meticulously researched and recreated in powerful prose.
claims.source: Publishers Weekly, unsigned review of River of Stars
claims.quote: meticulously researched and recreated in powerful prose

claims.claim: Publishers Weekly calls Under Heaven an exquisitely detailed vision of Kitan, a land much like Tang Dynasty China.
claims.source: Publishers Weekly, unsigned review of Under Heaven
claims.quote: an exquisitely detailed vision of Kitan

claims.claim: Publishers Weekly identifies the book's material as the complex intrigues of poets, prostitutes, ministers and soldiers.
claims.source: Publishers Weekly, unsigned review of Under Heaven
claims.quote: intrigues of poets, prostitutes, ministers, and soldiers

claims.claim: Publishers Weekly says Children of Earth and Sky is set in a world where nothing is as valuable as information.
claims.source: Publishers Weekly, unsigned review of Children of Earth and Sky
claims.quote: a world where nothing is as valuable as information

claims.claim: Publishers Weekly says the book offers an intricately detailed setting alongside marvelously believable characters.
claims.source: Publishers Weekly, unsigned review of Children of Earth and Sky
claims.quote: an intricately detailed setting, marvelously believable characters

claims.claim: Publishers Weekly says A Brightness Long Ago is narrated primarily by Guidanio Cerra, a clever young scholar.
claims.source: Publishers Weekly, unsigned review of A Brightness Long Ago
claims.quote: Narrated primarily by Guidanio Cerra, a clever young scholar

claims.claim: Publishers Weekly says Tigana brings to life a layered, pragmatic world of magic and difficult choices where brutality and beauty coexist.
claims.source: Publishers Weekly, unsigned review of Tigana
claims.quote: a layered, pragmatic world of magic and difficult choices

claims.claim: The Strange Horizons companion says Kay's foreshadowings and Crispin's awareness of ruins make the Sarantine Empire at its height seem vulnerable and transitory.
claims.source: Christopher Cobb and Mary Anne Mohanraj (unsigned companion), 'More about Guy Gavriel Kay's novels', Strange Horizons, 13 November 2000
claims.quote: seem vulnerable and transitory

claims.claim: Cilli says he was struck by the feel of Under Heaven, which had a very lyrical and poetic quality to it.
claims.source: Dominic Cilli, review of Under Heaven, SF Site, 2010
claims.quote: a very lyrical and poetic quality to it

claims.claim: James Seidman says it is amazing how many varied aspects of the historical Byzantine Empire are represented in Kay's fictional Sarantine Empire.
claims.source: James Seidman, review of Sailing to Sarantium, SF Site, 1999
claims.quote: how many varied aspects of the Byzantine Empire are represented

claims.claim: Seidman notes that among the obscure Byzantine features Kay carries over is a violent religious dispute mirroring the Arian heresy.
claims.source: James Seidman, review of Sailing to Sarantium, SF Site, 1999
claims.quote: a violent religious dispute that mirrors Christianity's Arian heresy

claims.claim: Wayne MacLaurin says every character from lowliest foot-soldier to high priest is rich and complex and seldom flat or misplaced.
claims.source: Wayne MacLaurin, review of Lord of Emperors, SF Site, 2000
claims.quote: from lowliest foot-soldier to high priest

claims.claim: MacLaurin says Sarantium itself comes to life within the pages of the novel.
claims.source: Wayne MacLaurin, review of Lord of Emperors, SF Site, 2000
claims.quote: Sarantium itself comes to life within the pages

claims.claim: Alma Hromic says Kay's books convey that history is woven from the small things done by and to people who live under the cloak of great events.
claims.source: Alma A. Hromic, review of The Last Light of the Sun, SF Site, 2004
claims.quote: history is woven from the small things

claims.claim: Hromic says Kay's minor characters pass through the book carrying some trace of events that have rolled across them.
claims.source: Alma A. Hromic, review of The Last Light of the Sun, SF Site, 2004
claims.quote: carry some trace of events that have rolled across them

claims.claim: Hromic says the book gives the sense of glimpsing a few shining threads in a larger tapestry.
claims.source: Alma A. Hromic, review of The Last Light of the Sun, SF Site, 2004
claims.quote: glimpsing a few shining threads in a larger tapestry

claims.claim: Hromic says there is the usual sense that more lies in the background of the story than the reader has been told.
claims.source: Alma A. Hromic, review of The Last Light of the Sun, SF Site, 2004
claims.quote: more, so much more, in the background

claims.claim: Michelle Sagara says Kay doesn't waste a word or a scene in The Lions of Al-Rassan and that there is no self-indulgent bloating.
claims.source: Michelle Sagara (Michelle West), review of The Lions of Al-Rassan for Quill & Quire (reprinted BrightWeavings)
claims.quote: Kay doesn't waste a word or a scene

claims.claim: Sagara says the possibilities of civilization developed at the height of the great cities are echoed bitterly by their fall.
claims.source: Michelle Sagara (Michelle West), review of The Lions of Al-Rassan for Quill & Quire (reprinted BrightWeavings)
claims.quote: are echoed bitterly by their fall

claims.claim: Doug Barbour says Kay creates rounded characters precisely by implying the social and psychological baggage they carry into every situation.
claims.source: Doug Barbour, review of The Lions of Al-Rassan for The Edmonton Journal (reprinted BrightWeavings)
claims.quote: precisely by implying all the social, as well as psychological, baggage

claims.claim: John H. Riskind says Kay's fantasy world has the ambience and sense of place of a fine historical novel.
claims.source: John H. Riskind, 'History with a Fantasy Spin', The Washington Post Book World (reprinted BrightWeavings)
claims.quote: the ambience and sense of place of a fine historical novel

claims.claim: Riskind says that in Kay's recent novels the supernatural or fantastic is subdued and relatively subtle, merely providing a backdrop.
claims.source: John H. Riskind, 'History with a Fantasy Spin', The Washington Post Book World (reprinted BrightWeavings)
claims.quote: subdued and relatively subtle, merely providing a backdrop

claims.claim: In a passage Riskind quotes, Kay reports an event becoming legend by being retold among physicians, courts, military companies, universities, taverns and places of worship.
claims.source: Guy Gavriel Kay, The Lions of Al-Rassan, quoted in John H. Riskind's Washington Post Book World review (reprinted BrightWeavings)
claims.quote: told so often among physicians, courts, military companies, in universities

claims.claim: Rob Kilheffer says Kay's contemporary outlook leads to some trouble with the tone of his prose.
claims.source: Rob Kilheffer, review of The Lions of Al-Rassan for Fantasy & Science Fiction (reprinted BrightWeavings)
claims.quote: some trouble with the tone of Kay's prose

claims.claim: Kilheffer says Kay mostly has the tone down well but every now and then his ear is a little off.
claims.source: Rob Kilheffer, review of The Lions of Al-Rassan for Fantasy & Science Fiction (reprinted BrightWeavings)
claims.quote: every now and then his ear is a little off

claims.claim: Kilheffer praises a scene in which King Ramiro converts his role using a reliance on written law and formal court hearings, general taxation and building projects.
claims.source: Rob Kilheffer, review of The Lions of Al-Rassan for Fantasy & Science Fiction (reprinted BrightWeavings)
claims.quote: a reliance on written law and formal court hearings

claims.claim: Kilheffer notes Kay shows the characteristic mangling of Asharite names in the mouths of Jaddites, ibn Musa becoming Abenmuza.
claims.source: Rob Kilheffer, review of The Lions of Al-Rassan for Fantasy & Science Fiction (reprinted BrightWeavings)
claims.quote: mangling of Arabic (Asharite) names in the mouths of Europeans

claims.claim: Kilheffer says Kay is overly fond of withholding information from the reader longer than might seem natural.
claims.source: Rob Kilheffer, review of The Lions of Al-Rassan for Fantasy & Science Fiction (reprinted BrightWeavings)
claims.quote: withholding information from the reader longer than might seem natural

claims.claim: Kilheffer says Kay leaves the show-duel off-stage and lets the reader glean what is known of it from scattered offhand references thereafter.
claims.source: Rob Kilheffer, review of The Lions of Al-Rassan for Fantasy & Science Fiction (reprinted BrightWeavings)
claims.quote: glean what we know of it from scattered offhand references

claims.claim: Kilheffer says that by so conspicuously leaving the action out Kay draws the reader's attention to the event more strongly than showing it entire.
claims.source: Rob Kilheffer, review of The Lions of Al-Rassan for Fantasy & Science Fiction (reprinted BrightWeavings)
claims.quote: by so conspicuously leaving the action out

claims.claim: Kilheffer says Kay is exceedingly adept at staging taut verbal exchanges, from courtly politicking to flirtatious innuendo.
claims.source: Rob Kilheffer, review of The Lions of Al-Rassan for Fantasy & Science Fiction (reprinted BrightWeavings)
claims.quote: exceedingly adept at staging taut verbal exchanges

claims.claim: Kilheffer says Kay handles the multiple viewpoints skilfully and uses them to add complexity to the world and the plot.
claims.source: Rob Kilheffer, review of The Lions of Al-Rassan for Fantasy & Science Fiction (reprinted BrightWeavings)
claims.quote: Kay handles these multiple viewpoints skilfully

claims.claim: Rob Kilheffer says there are no disposable people in The Lions of Al-Rassan, no fodder for the swords of the heroes.
claims.source: Rob Kilheffer, review of The Lions of Al-Rassan for Fantasy & Science Fiction (reprinted BrightWeavings)
claims.quote: there are no disposable people here

claims.claim: Dave Langford says that instead of prolonged generalized battle scenes Kay indicates the horror of war and tyranny in short, sharp scenes of atrocity.
claims.source: Dave Langford, review of The Lions of Al-Rassan for SFX Magazine (reprinted BrightWeavings)
claims.quote: in short, sharp scenes of atrocity

claims.claim: Langford says Kay's attention is always on individuals.
claims.source: Dave Langford, review of The Lions of Al-Rassan for SFX Magazine (reprinted BrightWeavings)
claims.quote: His attention is always on individuals

claims.claim: Jo Walton calls the Sarantine Mosaic's style an odd, distanced, elegaic style that she wants to call veiled omniscient.
claims.source: Jo Walton, reread of the Sarantine Mosaic (originally Tor.com, reprinted BrightWeavings)
claims.quote: an odd, distanced, elegaic style that I want to call

claims.claim: Walton says the omniscient narrator knows what will happen and what everyone thinks but does not like to approach too closely.
claims.source: Jo Walton, reread of the Sarantine Mosaic (originally Tor.com, reprinted BrightWeavings)
claims.quote: but doesn't like to approach too closely

claims.claim: Walton says of Kay's narrator that he draws and lifts veils.
claims.source: Jo Walton, reread of the Sarantine Mosaic (originally Tor.com, reprinted BrightWeavings)
claims.quote: He draws and lifts veils

claims.claim: Walton dislikes Kay's trick of describing a character without saying who it is, and says she hates it when Dorothy Dunnett does it too.
claims.source: Jo Walton, reread of the Sarantine Mosaic (originally Tor.com, reprinted BrightWeavings)
claims.quote: he described but doesn't say who is who

claims.claim: Walton says there is a sense that we are always looking through the wrong end of the telescope, that these people are far away.
claims.source: Jo Walton, reread of the Sarantine Mosaic (originally Tor.com, reprinted BrightWeavings)
claims.quote: looking through the wrong end of the telescope

claims.claim: Walton says the distanced manner sometimes makes for very beautiful writing but that there is always a pulling back.
claims.source: Jo Walton, reread of the Sarantine Mosaic (originally Tor.com, reprinted BrightWeavings)
claims.quote: but there's always a pulling back

claims.claim: Walton says the details are right for sixth century Byzantium and that even where Kay has made them up they feel right.
claims.source: Jo Walton, reread of the Sarantine Mosaic (originally Tor.com, reprinted BrightWeavings)
claims.quote: even where he's made them up they feel right

claims.claim: Walton says Kay mediates the world through the chariot races and the making of mosaics and often describes it in those terms.
claims.source: Jo Walton, reread of the Sarantine Mosaic (originally Tor.com, reprinted BrightWeavings)
claims.quote: mediates the world through the chariot races and the making

claims.claim: Walton says a chariot race is seen from the point of view of a driver, someone in the crowd, and an undercook for the Blue faction making soup.
claims.source: Jo Walton, reread of the Sarantine Mosaic (originally Tor.com, reprinted BrightWeavings)
claims.quote: an undercook for the Blue faction making soup

claims.claim: Walton says the small amount of magic runs glinting through everything else like the silver threads in shot silk.
claims.source: Jo Walton, reread of the Sarantine Mosaic (originally Tor.com, reprinted BrightWeavings)
claims.quote: like the silver threads in shot silk

claims.claim: Cheryl Morgan says the bulk of The Last Light of the Sun is about people and about a developing society.
claims.source: Cheryl Morgan, review of The Last Light of the Sun, Emerald City (reprinted BrightWeavings)
claims.quote: and about a developing society

claims.claim: Morgan says the title refers not only to the sun setting on the lands of the Cyngael but to the sun setting on a whole lifestyle.
claims.source: Cheryl Morgan, review of The Last Light of the Sun, Emerald City (reprinted BrightWeavings)
claims.quote: the sun setting on a whole lifestyle

claims.claim: In a passage Morgan reproduces, Kay marks a fairy's antiquity by having a character notice that she speaks Cyngael the way his grandfather had.
claims.source: Guy Gavriel Kay, The Last Light of the Sun, quoted in Cheryl Morgan's Emerald City review (reprinted BrightWeavings)
claims.quote: She spoke Cyngael the way his grandfather had

claims.claim: Pembroke College's report of Kay's 2021 Tolkien Lecture says the talk argued for the vital importance of the unsaid and the unexplained in fiction.
claims.source: Pembroke College, Oxford, news report on the 2021 J.R.R. Tolkien Lecture, 20 May 2021
claims.quote: the vital importance of the unsaid and the unexplained in fiction

claims.claim: Kay asked in the 2021 Tolkien Lecture how comfortable our responses to art are with mystery, as quoted by Pembroke College.
claims.source: Guy Gavriel Kay, quoted in Pembroke College, Oxford news report, 20 May 2021
claims.quote: how comfortable in our responses to art are we with mystery

claims.claim: Olley identifies the retrospective construction of history as one of Kay's chief thematic concerns across all his works.
claims.source: Katherine Olley, 'Guy Gavriel Kay: A Short Introduction', University of Oxford, 16 December 2020
claims.quote: The nature of history is retrospective construction

claims.claim: Olley says Kay chooses to focus on the smaller, more personal moments behind the scenes that shape larger historical events.
claims.source: Katherine Olley, 'Guy Gavriel Kay: A Short Introduction', University of Oxford, 16 December 2020
claims.quote: the smaller, more personal moments behind the scenes

claims.claim: Olley observes that Kay condenses the whole of the An Lushan rebellion in Under Heaven into an epilogue.
claims.source: Katherine Olley, 'Guy Gavriel Kay: A Short Introduction', University of Oxford, 16 December 2020
claims.quote: all of that is condensed into an epilogue

claims.claim: Olley says that once events become inevitable Kay largely leaves them to be supplied by the reader's imagination.
claims.source: Katherine Olley, 'Guy Gavriel Kay: A Short Introduction', University of Oxford, 16 December 2020
claims.quote: Once events become inevitable, he largely leaves them

claims.claim: Olley says Kay encourages reflection with the clarity of hindsight rather than building suspense.
claims.source: Katherine Olley, 'Guy Gavriel Kay: A Short Introduction', University of Oxford, 16 December 2020
claims.quote: to look back with the tragic clarity of hindsight

claims.claim: Olley says Kay's research is close enough that he seems to write around history rather than rewrite it.
claims.source: Katherine Olley, 'Guy Gavriel Kay: A Short Introduction', University of Oxford, 16 December 2020
claims.quote: not to rewrite history but to write around it

claims.claim: Olley attributes Kay's distinctive style to his ability to find power in quiet moments rather than brash heroic ones.
claims.source: Katherine Olley, 'Guy Gavriel Kay: A Short Introduction', University of Oxford, 16 December 2020
claims.quote: ability to find power in these quiet moments

claims.claim: Olley states that Kay is himself a poet as well as a novelist.
claims.source: Katherine Olley, 'Guy Gavriel Kay: A Short Introduction', University of Oxford, 16 December 2020
claims.quote: is himself a poet as well as a novelist

claims.claim: Olley states that Kay's fantasy novels often include poetic quotations that he writes himself.
claims.source: Katherine Olley, 'Guy Gavriel Kay: A Short Introduction', University of Oxford, 16 December 2020
claims.quote: fantasy works often include poetic quotations

claims.claim: Olley says embedded poetry in fantasy narrative works by allowing a change in register.
claims.source: Katherine Olley, 'Verse and Prose in Fantasy Literature', University of Oxford, 16 December 2020
claims.quote: By allowing for a change in register

claims.claim: Olley says poetic quotations in fantasy cluster around moments of particular narrative significance.
claims.source: Katherine Olley, 'Verse and Prose in Fantasy Literature', University of Oxford, 16 December 2020
claims.quote: poetic quotations, often cluster around moments of particular narrative significance

claims.claim: Olley says the closing verse lament in The Lions of Al-Rassan heightens the pathos of the moment.
claims.source: Katherine Olley, 'Verse and Prose in Fantasy Literature', University of Oxford, 16 December 2020
claims.quote: Breaking into poetry here heightens the pathos of the moment

claims.claim: Olley says the closing verse allows Kay to impart a sense of closure to the novel itself.
claims.source: Katherine Olley, 'Verse and Prose in Fantasy Literature', University of Oxford, 16 December 2020
claims.quote: it allows Kay to impart a sense of closure

claims.claim: Olley argues that in Kay the conclusion of the novel's themes is conveyed by form as much as by content.
claims.source: Katherine Olley, 'Verse and Prose in Fantasy Literature', University of Oxford, 16 December 2020
claims.quote: It's not just what Kaye writes, but how he writes it

claims.claim: Olley states that although worldbuilding is central to fantasy, readers do not want to feel they are reading an encyclopaedia.
claims.source: Katherine Olley, 'Verse and Prose in Fantasy Literature', University of Oxford, 16 December 2020
claims.quote: But we do not want to feel like we're reading an encyclopaedia

claims.claim: Olley says a deft author can use a verse quotation to educate the reader about a world's history and culture.
claims.source: Katherine Olley, 'Verse and Prose in Fantasy Literature', University of Oxford, 16 December 2020
claims.quote: to educate us about a world history and culture

claims.claim: Olley says imitating the ancient and medieval prosimetric form lends fantasy literature an air of authority and authenticity.
claims.source: Katherine Olley, 'Verse and Prose in Fantasy Literature', University of Oxford, 16 December 2020
claims.quote: an air of authority and authenticity

claims.claim: Olley says the prosimetric form arose partly out of a desire for an authoritative narrative voice.
claims.source: Katherine Olley, 'Verse and Prose in Fantasy Literature', University of Oxford, 16 December 2020
claims.quote: a desire for an authoritative narrative voice

claims.claim: Olley says the snatch of verse heard on arrival in Fionavar signposts a major shift in setting and tone without moving the characters.
claims.source: Katherine Olley, 'Verse and Prose in Fantasy Literature', University of Oxford, 16 December 2020
claims.quote: A major shift in setting and tone

claims.claim: Olley says verse whose subject is a distant legendary past establishes a sense of historical depth.
claims.source: Katherine Olley, 'Verse and Prose in Fantasy Literature', University of Oxford, 16 December 2020
claims.quote: establishes a sense of historical depth

claims.claim: Christine Fischer Guy writes that Kay was a poet first and still publishes poetry from time to time.
claims.source: Christine Fischer Guy, 'The Fantastic Worlds of Guy Gavriel Kay', Los Angeles Review of Books, 14 August 2016
claims.quote: he was a poet first

claims.claim: Kay says Dorothy Dunnett conveyed a character's intelligence in the Lymond books by having characters say things the reader does not understand.
claims.source: Guy Gavriel Kay, interviewed in Locus, 'Margins of History', 2025
claims.quote: say things the reader doesn't understand

claims.claim: Kay says the effect of Dunnett's withheld references in the moment is the impression that these are really smart people.
claims.source: Guy Gavriel Kay, interviewed in Locus, 'Margins of History', 2025
claims.quote: These are really smart people

claims.claim: Kay calls it tricky writing to convey the idea that a character is genuinely smart.
claims.source: Guy Gavriel Kay, interviewed in Locus, 'Margins of History', 2025
claims.quote: to convey the idea that a character is genuinely smart

claims.claim: Kay says he has long looked for the unwritten histories and the people at the margins of history.
claims.source: Guy Gavriel Kay, interviewed in Locus, 'Margins of History', 2025
claims.quote: looking for the unwritten histories, the people at the margins of history

claims.claim: Allsopp says Dunnett almost never shows events from Lymond's point of view.
claims.source: Niall Allsopp, 'Dorothy Dunnett's Lymond Chronicles', Slightly Foxed Issue 81, 2024
claims.quote: We almost never see events from Lymond's point of view

claims.claim: Allsopp says the reader can never guess what Lymond is thinking.
claims.source: Niall Allsopp, 'Dorothy Dunnett's Lymond Chronicles', Slightly Foxed Issue 81, 2024
claims.quote: we can never guess what he is thinking

claims.claim: Allsopp faults Dunnett for always including a clunky exposition scene in which a character recites the political situation.
claims.source: Niall Allsopp, 'Dorothy Dunnett's Lymond Chronicles', Slightly Foxed Issue 81, 2024
claims.quote: There is also always a clunky exposition scene

claims.claim: Allsopp says Dunnett's best writing has something of Muriel Spark's spikiness but none of Spark's compression.
claims.source: Niall Allsopp, 'Dorothy Dunnett's Lymond Chronicles', Slightly Foxed Issue 81, 2024
claims.quote: though none of Spark's compression

claims.claim: Kay says Children of Earth and Sky starts from the borderlands and the lives of not-powerful people.
claims.source: Guy Gavriel Kay, interviewed by Christine Fischer Guy, Los Angeles Review of Books, 14 August 2016
claims.quote: it takes place on the borderlands in the lives of not-powerful people

claims.claim: Rettino says the opening passage of Tigana reads like an entry in a chronicle and lends the novel a historical flavour.
claims.source: Matthew Rettino, 'Fantasies of History: Guy Gavriel Kay's Synthesis of the Historical Fantasy Novel', 2012 McGill honours thesis, hosted at brightweavings.com
claims.quote: The opening passage reads like an entry in a chronicle

claims.claim: Rettino says Kay's narrator has a voice that at times resembles a historian's in its distanced relation of events.
claims.source: Matthew Rettino, 'Fantasies of History', 2012 McGill honours thesis, hosted at brightweavings.com
claims.quote: whose voice at times resembles that of a historian

claims.claim: Rettino says the revelation that Duke Sandre faked his death throws doubt on the reliability of the narrator's historian persona in Tigana.
claims.source: Matthew Rettino, 'Fantasies of History', 2012 McGill honours thesis, hosted at brightweavings.com
claims.quote: the reliability of the historian persona of the narrator

claims.claim: Rettino says that when Kay's narratorial voice reveals itself it adopts the authority of the club-story teller and becomes unquestionable.
claims.source: Matthew Rettino, 'Fantasies of History', 2012 McGill honours thesis, hosted at brightweavings.com
claims.quote: it adopts the authority of the club-story teller

claims.claim: Rettino says the omniscient historian's voice in The Lions of Al-Rassan prevents the novel from being a perfectly immersive fantasy.
claims.source: Matthew Rettino, 'Fantasies of History', 2012 McGill honours thesis, hosted at brightweavings.com
claims.quote: due to the narrator's omniscient historian's voice

claims.claim: Rettino says the narrator of Under Heaven presents himself as one Kitan historian among many.
claims.source: Matthew Rettino, 'Fantasies of History', 2012 McGill honours thesis, hosted at brightweavings.com
claims.quote: The narrator presents himself as one Kitan historian among many

claims.claim: Rettino says the narrator of Under Heaven places value on the scholarly consensus of the chronicles he cites.
claims.source: Matthew Rettino, 'Fantasies of History', 2012 McGill honours thesis, hosted at brightweavings.com
claims.quote: the narrator places value on the consensus, like a scholar

claims.claim: Rettino says that because not all documents survive in Under Heaven one cannot have a complete and therefore authoritative narrative of history.
claims.source: Matthew Rettino, 'Fantasies of History', 2012 McGill honours thesis, hosted at brightweavings.com
claims.quote: one cannot possibly have a complete and therefore authoritative narrative of history

claims.claim: Rettino says Kay's omniscient narrator subverts authoritative historical narration by revealing that many events in history are not known.
claims.source: Matthew Rettino, 'Fantasies of History', 2012 McGill honours thesis, hosted at brightweavings.com
claims.quote: many events in history are not known

claims.claim: Rettino says Kay implies that history is always crafted and that narratives are always imposed on recorded facts.
claims.source: Matthew Rettino, 'Fantasies of History', 2012 McGill honours thesis, hosted at brightweavings.com
claims.quote: history is always crafted

claims.claim: Rettino says historical fantasy in Kay can recover parts of history that have been lost through the omissions of historians.
claims.source: Matthew Rettino, 'Fantasies of History', 2012 McGill honours thesis, hosted at brightweavings.com
claims.quote: recover parts of history that have been lost

claims.claim: Rettino says Kay's poetry is only a small departure from his novels, given the lyricism of his prose.
claims.source: Matthew Rettino, review of Beyond this Dark House, matthewrettino.com, 7 February 2014
claims.quote: a departure from the grand quasi-historical narratives that define his novels

claims.claim: Rettino argues that the two moons in the title poem of Beyond this Dark House are not an allusion to Kay's novels but a slight suggestion about the beloved.
claims.source: Matthew Rettino, review of Beyond this Dark House, matthewrettino.com, 7 February 2014
claims.quote: two moons are no cheap allusion to his novels

claims.claim: Macpherson says Dunnett breaks the rules of point of view by rarely letting Lymond's sneering mask drop to reveal the man behind it.
claims.source: Marie Macpherson, 'A Riddle wrapped in a Mystery inside an Enigma', The Writers' Writer, Dorothy Dunnett Centenary (Dorothy Dunnett Society)
claims.quote: rarely letting her anti-hero's sneering mask drop

claims.claim: Macpherson says Lymond is seen through the eyes of others who constantly change their minds about him, as does the reader.
claims.source: Marie Macpherson, The Writers' Writer, Dorothy Dunnett Centenary (Dorothy Dunnett Society)
claims.quote: seen through the eyes of others who constantly change their minds

claims.claim: Macpherson says that despite the wealth of historical knowledge in her work Dunnett never descends into information dumping.
claims.source: Marie Macpherson, The Writers' Writer, Dorothy Dunnett Centenary (Dorothy Dunnett Society)
claims.quote: Dunnett never descends into information dumping

claims.claim: Macpherson attributes to Dunnett a painter's eye for detail that makes her descriptions of scenes linger long after reading.
claims.source: Marie Macpherson, The Writers' Writer, Dorothy Dunnett Centenary (Dorothy Dunnett Society)
claims.quote: Her painter's eye for gorgeous detail enlivens descriptions so striking

claims.claim: The screenwriter Gwyneth Hughes reports that even reading the Lymond Chronicles in order there were stretches where she had no idea what was going on.
claims.source: Gwyneth Hughes, The Writers' Writer, Dorothy Dunnett Centenary (Dorothy Dunnett Society)
claims.quote: stretches where I had no idea what was going on

claims.claim: Ellen Kushner says she became obsessed with Dunnett's technique, knowing she was pulling all sorts of tricks without being able to see how.
claims.source: Ellen Kushner, The Writers' Writer, Dorothy Dunnett Centenary (Dorothy Dunnett Society)
claims.quote: I knew she was pulling all sorts of tricks

claims.claim: Ellen Kushner says she wrote Swordspoint, in conversation with the Lymond Chronicles, keeping the narrative as spare and devious as possible.
claims.source: Ellen Kushner, The Writers' Writer, Dorothy Dunnett Centenary (Dorothy Dunnett Society)
claims.quote: keeping the narrative as spare and devious as possible

claims.claim: Kay says poetry in many languages and music are inextricably bound up with Dunnett's writing.
claims.source: Guy Gavriel Kay, 'In Memoriam - Dorothy Dunnett', Locus Magazine, December 2001, reproduced at brightweavings.com
claims.quote: Poetry (in many languages) and music are inextricably bound up

claims.claim: Kay says Dunnett's books are filled to overflowing with music and verse.
claims.source: Guy Gavriel Kay, 'In Memoriam - Dorothy Dunnett', Locus Magazine, December 2001, reproduced at brightweavings.com
claims.quote: The books are filled - gloriously so, spilling over

claims.claim: Kay says the principal reason the language of the Fionavar Tapestry differs from his later books is that it was his mythic endeavour.
claims.source: Guy Gavriel Kay, 'The Fionavar Tapestry Afterword', HarperPerennial Canada 20th anniversary edition, December 2003, reproduced at brightweavings.com
claims.quote: the language of the trilogy differs from my later books

claims.claim: Kay says his later books track a movement, not a consistent one, towards history.
claims.source: Guy Gavriel Kay, 'The Fionavar Tapestry Afterword', December 2003, reproduced at brightweavings.com
claims.quote: The others track a movement (not a consistent one) towards history

claims.claim: Kay says the language of the Fionavar Tapestry was guided by the matter of the story, a god imprisoned under a mountain and a battle beneath a sacrificial tree.
claims.source: Guy Gavriel Kay, 'The Fionavar Tapestry Afterword', December 2003, reproduced at brightweavings.com
claims.quote: Language was guided by that context

claims.claim: Kay says he does not believe in saying exactly what happens to characters after a novel closes, and that the ending of every book he has written makes this point.
claims.source: Guy Gavriel Kay, 'The Fionavar Tapestry Afterword', December 2003, reproduced at brightweavings.com
claims.quote: saying exactly what happens to characters after a novel closes

claims.claim: Kay says we do not always know what happens next, in life or fiction, and the end of a novel does not demand tying down every life that passed through it.
claims.source: Guy Gavriel Kay, 'The Fionavar Tapestry Afterword', December 2003, reproduced at brightweavings.com
claims.quote: we don't always know what happens next, in life or fiction

claims.claim: Kay says he cut a planned closing conversation for Sharra because the scene felt static and flat, existing only to tie up a thread.
claims.source: Guy Gavriel Kay, 'The Fionavar Tapestry Afterword', December 2003, reproduced at brightweavings.com
claims.quote: The scene felt static, flat

claims.claim: The Dorothy Dunnett Society reports that the memorial stone in Edinburgh's Makars' Court carries a quotation from Dunnett asking where the links in the chain joining us to the past are.
claims.source: Dorothy Dunnett Society, 'Dorothy Dunnett' biography page
claims.quote: the links in the chain … joining us to the past

claims.claim: The Dorothy Dunnett Society describes the House of Niccolo novels as containing poetry and music wrapped up in an evocation of history.
claims.source: Dorothy Dunnett Society, 'Dorothy Dunnett' biography page
claims.quote: poetry and music, all wrapped up in an evocation of history

claims.claim: The Dorothy Dunnett Society's magazine publishes essays studying hints in Dunnett's text to establish what a character's purpose was.
claims.source: Dorothy Dunnett Society, Whispering Gallery page describing Issue 166 (June 2025)
claims.quote: we study the hints in the text that suggest

claims.claim: The Dorothy Dunnett Society calls the question of which child died during the chess game at Topkapi a perennial argument among readers.
claims.source: Dorothy Dunnett Society, Whispering Gallery page describing Issue 166 (June 2025)
claims.quote: We revisit a perennial argument in this issue

claims.claim: The Dunnett close-reader 'bill' identifies Dunnett's habit of having one character's assessment explain to the reader what has already taken place, calling it an interesting writing technique.
claims.source: bill, 'The Play for Jonathan Crouch - III. More Blindfold Play', Bill's Dunnett Blog (dorothydunnett.co.uk), 9 July 2026
claims.quote: an interesting writing technique

claims.claim: The Dunnett close-reader 'bill' says Sybilla's assessment is what explains to the reader what has taken place.
claims.source: bill, 'The Play for Jonathan Crouch - III. More Blindfold Play', Bill's Dunnett Blog, 9 July 2026
claims.quote: her assessment also explains what has taken place to the reader

claims.claim: The Dunnett close-reader 'bill' says there are always so many layers to what Dunnett is telling the reader, after listing unanswered questions raised by one exchange.
claims.source: bill, 'The Play for Jonathan Crouch - IV: Several Moves by a Knight', Bill's Dunnett Blog, 5 August 2026
claims.quote: Always so many layers to what Dorothy is telling us

claims.claim: The Dunnett close-reader 'bill' says the Game of Kings is written so that the reader realises nothing is ever quite what it seems.
claims.source: bill, 'The Play for Jonathan Crouch - V: Castling', Bill's Dunnett Blog, 21 August 2026
claims.quote: nothing is ever quite what it seems

claims.claim: The Dunnett close-reader 'bill' says new readers are told that at about a hundred pages in they will change their mind on everything that has confused them.
claims.source: bill, 'The Play for Jonathan Crouch - V: Castling', Bill's Dunnett Blog, 21 August 2026
claims.quote: everything that has confused them up till now

claims.claim: Fréchette states that Vonarburg rendered Kay's Guinevere by the modern French form rather than the older Guenièvre.
claims.source: Amélie Fréchette, mémoire de maîtrise, Université Laval, 2013, note 42
claims.quote: par le nom français moderne

claims.claim: Kay writes that the narrator Simon Vance sent him a note about needing to pause at times to control emotion while reading Children of Earth and Sky aloud.
claims.source: Guy Gavriel Kay, Brightweavings journal, Children of Earth and Sky
claims.quote: needing to pause at times to control emotion as he read

claims.claim: Kay says he often makes adjustments to his text after reading his writing aloud.
claims.source: Guy Gavriel Kay, Brightweavings journal, Children of Earth and Sky
claims.quote: I often make adjustments after doing that.

claims.claim: Kay says that adding a semi-colon or too many technically viable commas to a passage of rapid, stressed speech undermines the effect of the passage.
claims.source: Guy Gavriel Kay, Brightweavings Ysabel journal, 2006
claims.quote: undermines the EFFECT of the passage

claims.claim: Vonarburg says that seeing multiple points of view in practice through what Kay does with them, and writing them herself while translating, was different from knowing the theory.
claims.source: Élisabeth Vonarburg, interviewed by Yann Etienne, Diacritik, 19 February 2021
claims.quote: les voir en pratique à travers ce qu’en fait Kay

claims.claim: Kattnig asserts that Kay's writing is not an end in itself and serves his story.
claims.source: Alain Kattnig, Éditions L'Atalante blog, 4 July 2014
claims.quote: L’écriture de Guy Gavriel Kay n’est pas une fin et sert son histoire.

claims.claim: Gillossen asserts that Kay's style seems to merge with the people he is treating, according to that people's own characteristics.
claims.source: Gillossen, critique of Les Derniers Feux du soleil, Elbakin.net, 19 April 2009
claims.quote: Son style semble se confondre avec le peuple qu'il aborde

claims.claim: Gillossen argues that the prose of The Last Light of the Sun becoming less subtle is deliberate, to sharpen the contrast with the sophisticated culture of Sarantium.
claims.source: Gillossen, critique of Les Derniers Feux du soleil, Elbakin.net, 19 April 2009
claims.quote: sa prose se fait moins subtile

claims.claim: Siriane describes Kay's tendency to cut the narration in the middle of a scene in order to pull back into more philosophical considerations.
claims.source: Siriane, critique of Children of Earth and Sky, Elbakin.net, 20 January 2017
claims.quote: couper la narration sur le vif de telle ou telle scène

claims.claim: Siriane writes that in this book Kay seems less interested in the events themselves than in their impact.
claims.source: Siriane, critique of Children of Earth and Sky, Elbakin.net, 20 January 2017
claims.quote: moins intéressé par les évènements eux-mêmes que leur impact

claims.claim: Simon Vance names Guy Gavriel Kay's work among his favourite narration projects.
claims.source: Simon Vance, interviewed for Vocal Media's Interview channel
claims.quote: I have always loved narrating the work of Guy Gavriel Kay
